passages.text: Bibi Gulab Kaur was the leader of Ghadar Party in Manila, Philippines. She and her husband Mann Singh sailed from the Philippines to India in order to rally the masses against British tyranny. Besides spreading anti-British public sentiment, she distributed literature relating to freedom movement, arms and ammunition to the members of Ghadar Party. Under sedition charges, she was kept in the notorious Lahore Fort and tortured for two years. Gulab Kaur was born in 1890 in the village of Bakshi Wala in the Sangrur region of Punjab in a poor peasant family. She was married to Mann Singh. This was a time when many Punjabi farmers were expelled from their land by British policy. The couple departed for Manila, Philippines with the intention of emigrating to the United States of America in order to escape economic troubles in their own country. Gulab Kaur joined the fight to oust the British in India and became one of the key Gadhar party members. She travelled around the Philippines in order to organise the Indian citizens. Moreover, she gathered weapons and funds for the party. She mobilised people in Manila and inspired them to join the party by distributing independence literature and delivering inspiring speeches to Indian passengers of ships.

Donkeys may be the proverbial beast of burden, and the animal itself has come to symbolise a dimwit, someone of little value. But not all donkeys are created equal. The Halari donkeys, a breed native to Gujarat's Halar region, is not just valued, it is a VVIP. The Halari donkey is a source of 'liquid gold', with its milk, valued for its distinctive properties, known to have sold for an astounding Rs 5000 to Rs 7000 per litre at some online platforms. But this acclaim comes with its own set of challenges. With fewer than 500 Halari donkeys remaining, the primary need is, of course, conservation. But the larger aim is not just increasing their numbers; it's about teaching farmers the best practices, so that they can command premium prices. Recognising the pressing need for conservation, the National Research Centre on Equines (NRCE) in Bikaner has started a dedicated programme to safeguard these animals. NRCE is also evaluating donkey milk for potential use in skincare products to sustain its value. The Halari donkey is not just valued for its milk; its unique characteristics make it particularly valuable for sustainable dairy farming. Their docile nature, combined with their adaptability to various climates, makes them ideal for small-scale farmers. They also have a much lower environmental foot-print, compared to larger livestock, requiring less feed and water. In fact, their grazing habits even help maintain grassland ecosystems.

The stranger came early in February, one wintry day, through a biting wind and a driving snow, the last snowfall of the year, over the down, walking from Bramblehurst railway station, carrying a little black portmanteau in his thickly gloved hand. He was wrapped up from head to foot, and the brim of his soft felt hat hid every inch of his face but the shiny tip of his nose; the snow had piled itself against his shoulders and chest, and added a white crest to the burden he carried. He staggered into the 'Coach and Horses' more dead than alive, and flung his portmanteau down. 'A fire,' he cried, 'in the name of human charity! A room and a fire!' He stamped and shook the snow off from himself in the bar, and followed Mrs. Hall into her guest parlour to strike his bargain. And with that much introduction, and a couple of sovereigns flung upon the table, he took up his quarters in the inn. Mrs. Hall lit the fire and left him there while she went to prepare him a meal with her own hands. A guest to stop at Iping in winter time was an unheard-of piece of luck, let alone a guest who was no 'haggler,' and she was resolved to show herself worthy of her good fortune.

questions.text: City planners across the world are rediscovering an old ally: the tree. As concrete spreads and summers grow harsher, urban heat islands - pockets where temperatures run several degrees higher than the surrounding countryside - have become a public-health concern. Studies show that a mature tree canopy can lower surface temperatures by as much as five degrees, filtering pollutants and shading pedestrians at the same time. Yet planting alone is not enough. Municipalities that ignore maintenance often watch saplings die within two seasons, wasting public money and public trust. Experts therefore argue for a 'whole-life' approach: budgeting for watering, pruning and soil care for at least five years after planting. Cities such as Singapore and Melbourne have adopted canopy targets, committing to raise tree cover to thirty percent or more by 2040. Critics caution, however, that targets must not become mere photo opportunities; a tree counted on a dashboard is not the same as a tree shading a bus stop. The measure of an urban forest, they insist, is not how many saplings are planted but how many survive, grow, and cool the streets beneath them.

In a quiet cluster of villages near Kanchipuram, the click of wooden looms still marks the hours. Weavers here produce silk saris whose motifs - temple borders, mango buttis - carry meanings older than any written record. Each sari takes nearly three weeks to complete, and the weaver's family often works as a single unit: the husband at the loom, the wife winding thread, the children counting patterns. Despite this skill, earnings remain thin. Middlemen capture much of the final price, and power-loom imitations flood markets at a third of the cost. The Geographical Indication (GI) tag, awarded to Kanchipuram silk in 2005, was meant to protect authenticity. In practice, enforcement is weak; a shopper in a city mall can rarely tell a genuine handloom sari from a machine-made copy. Weavers' cooperatives now attempt direct online sales, cutting out middlemen entirely. Early results are promising but modest. As one elder weaver puts it, 'The loom feeds us, but only if the world knows our name.'

Why do we forget most of what we study within days? Cognitive scientists point to a surprising answer: sleep. During deep sleep, the hippocampus replays the day's experiences to the neocortex, effectively transferring fragile memories into stable long-term storage. Students who revise late into the night and then cut sleep short sabotage precisely the process that would have consolidated their learning. Experiments consistently show that participants who sleep eight hours after learning outperform those who stay awake, even when total study time is identical. Naps help too, though briefly. Researchers caution, however, that sleep is not a magic eraser of poor study habits; spacing, retrieval practice and attention still matter. The practical lesson is unglamorous: treat sleep as part of the syllabus, not as a reward for finishing it.
